gse_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Edge engine the book maps onto the full stack: least squares and ridge as the baseline projection layer, L1 sparsity as the feature demotion mechanism, walk-forward hold-out and blocked cross-validation as the only promotion evidence, bias-variance accounting on every error report, ensembles chosen by error decorrelation, kernel similarity over situations with Gaussian process style uncertainty that grows away from observed matchups, Bayesian posteriors over team strength that update game by game, generative typicality checks on incoming situations, and subgroup performance reports that respect the fairness impossibility constraint. Nothing in the mapping concerns wagering mechanics; it is entirely about how projections are built, evidenced and bounded.
gsi_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Institute this book is curriculum-grade foundations: it supplies the shared vocabulary (E_new, bias-variance, regularisation, kernels, posteriors) and the shared standards of evidence that let researchers in different lanes compare claims. Its teaching value is the insistence that evaluation design precedes model design, that leakage is a data crime rather than a modelling detail, and that impossibility results, like the fairness theorem, are knowledge to design around rather than obstacles to argue with. It belongs in the institute library as the reference against which new methods papers are checked for what they assume and what they actually prove.

assumptions: Training data consists of input-output pairs drawn as independent samples
The relationship between input and output is too complicated or unknown to be written as an explicit rule-based program
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when data points are not independent, for example time series where consecutive samples are correlated; the book explicitly restricts itself to independent data points

layer2.mapping: The engine is a supervised learner over historical game examples: features are the input, outcomes and performance measures are the output, and every model in the stack inherits this contract of learning from examples instead of hand-coded rules
layer2.telemetry: Labelled historical game records with feature vectors and realised outcomes

primitives.name: Supervised learning: learn an input-output relationship from labelled examples rather than from explicit rules
primitives.verbatim_quote: In other words, supervised machine learning amounts to learning from examples.

assumptions: Closeness in the chosen distance implies similarity of outputs
Inputs are scaled so that Euclidean distance is meaningful across coordinates
primitives.breakdown_regime: Degrades in high dimensions where distances concentrate, and with k = 1 it is maximally sensitive to label noise; prediction cost grows with the full training set because nothing is compressed into parameters

layer2.mapping: Analog and comparable-game retrieval in the reasoning engine is k-NN logic: a projection for a new matchup is anchored on the most similar historical situations, and the similarity metric choice is a modelling decision, not a default
layer2.telemetry: Distance or similarity scores between the current matchup feature vector and historical matchup vectors

primitives.name: k-nearest neighbours: predict by averaging (regression) or majority vote (classification) over the k closest training points; the training data is kept and used at prediction time

symbol_and_unit_ledger.N_star: index set of the k training points closest to x_star under the chosen distance
symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_star: test input vector, same units as training inputs
symbol_and_unit_ledger.y_j: output of neighbour j, output units

primitives.verbatim_quote: Methods that explicitly use the training data when making predictions are referred to as nonparametric

assumptions: Axis-aligned threshold rules on single variables are expressive enough for the problem
A constant per region is an adequate local model
primitives.breakdown_regime: Greedy recursive splitting makes early split choices that can be suboptimal later; deep trees overfit (high variance), shallow trees underfit, and smooth diagonal boundaries need many splits to approximate

layer2.mapping: Situational splits in the engine (rest differentials, surface, game script buckets) are tree regions: the reasoning layer should treat each region as carrying its own local base rate rather than one global rate
layer2.telemetry: Counts and outcome rates per situational region or leaf bucket

primitives.name: Decision trees partition the input space into disjoint axis-aligned regions by recursive binary splits, with a constant prediction in each leaf region

symbol_and_unit_ledger.M: number of leaf regions, dimensionless count
symbol_and_unit_ledger.R_m: m-th leaf region of the input space, defined by the split rules on the path from the root
symbol_and_unit_ledger.y_m hat: constant prediction in region m, output units

primitives.verbatim_quote: The decision tree effectively divides the input space into multiple disjoint regions, and in each region, a constant value is used for the prediction

assumptions: The output is an affine function of the inputs plus noise with mean zero independent of the input
X^T X is invertible, which requires more data points than parameters and no exact collinearity
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails under collinearity or p >= n where the normal equations have no unique solution, and whenever the true relationship is strongly non-linear in the raw inputs

layer2.mapping: The engine's linear baseline layer: any projection model should be benchmarked against the closed-form least squares fit on the same features, because it is the cheapest exact optimum and exposes whether added complexity earns anything
layer2.telemetry: Design matrices of matchup features and realised outcome vectors

primitives.name: Linear regression models the output as an affine combination of inputs plus zero-mean noise, and least squares learning solves the normal equations in closed form

symbol_and_unit_ledger.X: n by (p+1) design matrix of training inputs with a leading column of ones, input units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.n: number of training points, dimensionless count
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p: number of input variables, dimensionless count
symbol_and_unit_ledger.theta hat: learned parameter vector of length p+1, output units per input unit
symbol_and_unit_ledger.y: n-vector of training outputs, output units

primitives.verbatim_quote: Regression is one of the two fundamental tasks of supervised learning (the other one is classification).

assumptions: Squared error loss
Shrinking all parameters toward zero is an acceptable prior preference
The intercept handling follows the book's convention of penalising the full parameter vector
primitives.breakdown_regime: Lambda = 0 recovers unregularised least squares with its singularity problems; lambda too large forces all parameters to zero and destroys fit; lambda must be tuned, typically by cross-validation

layer2.mapping: Shrinkage in the engine's rating updates is ridge logic: new evidence moves a rating only in proportion to a penalty on movement, which guarantees a stable unique update even when a team has few observations
layer2.telemetry: Per-team observation counts and feature collinearity diagnostics

primitives.name: L2 regularisation (ridge) adds lambda times the squared parameter norm to the least squares cost and always yields a unique closed-form solution for lambda > 0

symbol_and_unit_ledger.X, y, theta hat: as in the least squares primitive
symbol_and_unit_ledger.n: number of training points, dimensionless count

primitives.verbatim_quote: When XT X is not invertible, the ordinary normal equations (3.13) have no unique solution

assumptions: Squared error loss
A sparse explanation is plausible for the problem
No closed form exists, so a numerical optimisation algorithm is required
primitives.breakdown_regime: Among strongly correlated inputs the LASSO choice of which one survives is unstable; lambda too large zeroes out genuinely informative inputs

layer2.mapping: Feature pruning in the engine should be sparsity-driven: a signal family that an L1 penalty repeatedly switches off across validation windows is a candidate for demotion, with the zeroing itself recorded as the evidence
layer2.telemetry: Per-feature coefficient paths as the penalty varies across validation folds

primitives.name: L1 regularisation (LASSO) favours sparse solutions with many parameters exactly zero, so it performs input selection as a side effect of fitting

symbol_and_unit_ledger.X, y, n: as in the least squares primitive
symbol_and_unit_ledger.||theta||_1: sum of absolute parameter values, mixed units by parameter

primitives.verbatim_quote: and it can therefore be used as an input (or feature) selection method.

assumptions: The model is trained by an iterative numerical optimisation
A hold-out set is available and its error is monitored after each iteration
Hold-out error typically decreases first and then increases while training cost keeps decreasing
primitives.breakdown_regime: Noisy hold-out curves make the stopping point unstable; with very small hold-out sets the minimum is poorly located, and the method does nothing for closed-form models

layer2.mapping: Iterative calibration procedures in the engine need a stopping rule tied to held-out performance rather than to training fit; continued fitting past the hold-out minimum is overfitting by definition in this framework
layer2.telemetry: Hold-out error trace per iteration of any iterative fitting procedure

primitives.name: Early stopping is implicit regularisation: abort iterative optimisation when hold-out error stops decreasing, before the cost function reaches its minimum
primitives.verbatim_quote: It amounts to aborting the optimisation before it has reached the minimum of the cost function.

assumptions: New data is drawn from the same distribution p(x, y) as the training data
An error function appropriate to the task has been fixed
primitives.breakdown_regime: E_new can never be computed exactly in practice because p(x, y) is unknown; under distribution shift between training and deployment it is not even the right target

layer2.mapping: The engine's scoreboard is E_new thinking: only performance on games not used in fitting counts as evidence, and in-sample fit statistics are explicitly not performance claims
layer2.telemetry: Out-of-sample prediction errors logged per game with the model version and training window recorded

primitives.name: E_new, the expected error on new unseen data drawn from p(x, y), is the quantity supervised learning actually optimises; training error does not estimate it

symbol_and_unit_ledger.E(., .): error function comparing prediction and realised output
symbol_and_unit_ledger.E_new: expected new data error, error-function units (0-1 for misclassification, squared output units for squared error)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.E_star: expectation over test points drawn from p(x, y)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.T: the training dataset the model was learned from

primitives.verbatim_quote: In the end, supervised machine learning amounts to designing a method which performs well when faced with an endless stream of new, unseen data.

assumptions: Training and hold-out points are drawn from the same distribution
The split is made randomly, since an ordered dataset can put one class in training and the other in validation
primitives.breakdown_regime: Large hold-out sets shrink training data and raise E_new itself; small hold-out sets give a high-variance estimate; repeated model selection on the same hold-out overfits it

layer2.mapping: Walk-forward evaluation in the engine is the hold-out idea sequenced over time: each evaluation window is untouched by fitting, and the estimate's variance shrinks only with more evaluated games, which caps how fine a performance difference can be claimed
layer2.telemetry: Per-window out-of-sample errors and window sizes

primitives.name: Hold-out validation error is an unbiased estimate of E_new computed on data used neither for training nor, ideally, repeatedly for decisions

symbol_and_unit_ledger.T: training data excluding the hold-out set
symbol_and_unit_ledger.n_v: number of hold-out points, dimensionless count

primitives.verbatim_quote: A remedy is to set aside some hold-out validation data

assumptions: Folds are formed randomly from data drawn from one distribution
A separate untouched test set is still required for a final unbiased performance estimate
primitives.breakdown_regime: Costs k full trainings; random folds leak information when data points are grouped or time-ordered, so grouped or blocked folds are required in those regimes; cross-validation does not remove overfitting risk in model selection

layer2.mapping: Season-blocked cross-validation is the engine's hyperparameter selection mechanism: folds respect season and week boundaries so that no fold's evaluation games share a leakage path with its training games
layer2.telemetry: Per-fold out-of-sample errors for each candidate hyperparameter setting

primitives.name: k-fold cross-validation estimates E_new by rotating the hold-out role across k folds, so all data is used for both training and evaluation without a permanent validation set

symbol_and_unit_ledger.E_hold-out^(k): hold-out error of the model trained without fold k, evaluated on fold k, error units

primitives.verbatim_quote: validation instead of putting aside hold-out validation data; the idea of how to use it in the iterative procedure is unchanged.

assumptions: Squared error loss
Outputs are generated as a true function plus independent zero-mean noise
The decomposition is stated for regression; for classification it is intuition rather than an exact identity
primitives.breakdown_regime: The irreducible term cannot be reduced by any model; bias is roughly fixed by model class while variance grows as training data shrinks, so small-sample regimes are variance-dominated

layer2.mapping: Every engine error report should be decomposable in these terms: a systematic miss across many games is bias (model class problem), scatter across similar games is variance (data or flexibility problem), and the residual floor is the sport's inherent unpredictability, which no signal can remove
layer2.telemetry: Signed error means and error variances per model family across evaluation windows

primitives.name: Expected new data error decomposes into squared bias plus variance plus irreducible noise; model complexity trades the first two against each other

symbol_and_unit_ledger.E_T: expectation over training sets drawn from p(x, y)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f bar: average model over all possible training sets of size n, output units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.sigma^2: irreducible noise variance, squared output units

primitives.verbatim_quote: The main point here is that to obtain a small expected squared error, we have to consider both the bias and the variance.

assumptions: Data points belong to identifiable groups within which points are correlated
Deployment data will contain new groups, not new points from training groups
primitives.breakdown_regime: Random point-level splits silently leak; the failure is invisible in validation numbers and only appears as a production drop, which is why the book insists the split unit must match the deployment unit

layer2.mapping: In the engine the group is the game and the team-season: plays or games from the same matchup must never straddle a train and validation split, and team identity itself is a grouping variable when estimating how the model treats unseen opponents
layer2.telemetry: Split manifests showing group identifiers assigned wholly to one side of each split

primitives.name: Group leakage: when data points come in correlated groups, splits must be made over groups, not points, or validation performance is optimistically biased
primitives.verbatim_quote: Group leakage can occur if the data points are not really stochastically independent but are ordered into different groups.

assumptions: The input-output relationship is a composition of affine maps and scalar non-linearities
Enough data exists to fit a parameter count far larger than a linear model's
primitives.breakdown_regime: No closed-form training exists; optimisation is non-convex, parameter dimension is huge, and without regularisation or early stopping the model overfits small datasets

layer2.mapping: The engine's learned feature interactions are layered compositions: raw situational variables enter, hidden combinations form matchup-level features, and the output layer prices them; depth is justified only when the composed features beat the linear baseline out of sample
layer2.telemetry: Training and hold-out loss curves per architecture candidate

primitives.name: A neural network stacks layers of generalised linear models: parallel units apply an activation to an affine combination, and layers compose these transformations

symbol_and_unit_ledger.U: number of hidden units, dimensionless count
symbol_and_unit_ledger.W^(1), W^(2): first and second layer weight matrices, mixed units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.h: activation function, maps real line to real line

primitives.verbatim_quote: We first make use of several parallel generalised linear regression models to build a layer (which will lead us to the two-layer neural network) and then stack these layers in a sequential construction (which will result in a deep neural network).

assumptions: Units share the same activation within a layer in the book's presentation
Inputs are scaled so pre-activations sit in a useful range of the activation
primitives.breakdown_regime: Saturating activations stall gradient-based learning at extreme inputs; ReLU units can die permanently at zero output; a network of purely linear activations collapses to a single linear model

layer2.mapping: Bounded versus unbounded response shapes matter in engine features: saturating transforms suit probability-like signals, while ReLU-style transforms suit accumulating counting signals; choosing the response shape is choosing how a signal is allowed to grow
layer2.telemetry: Distributions of pre-activation values per feature transform

primitives.name: Activation functions supply the non-linearity: the logistic function saturates between 0 and 1, while ReLU is the identity for positive inputs and zero otherwise and is the modern default

symbol_and_unit_ledger.h(z): unit output, in (0,1) for logistic and [0, infinity) for ReLU
symbol_and_unit_ledger.z: pre-activation affine combination, dimensionless after scaling

primitives.verbatim_quote: Common choices of activation function are the logistic function and the rectified linear unit (ReLU).

assumptions: Outputs are categorical with a known set of M classes
The model produces one logit per class and a softmax link
primitives.breakdown_regime: Cross-entropy is unbounded for confidently wrong predictions, so label noise and outliers dominate training unless the data is cleaned or the loss is modified

layer2.mapping: Win-probability heads in the engine are trained and scored in log-loss terms: a confidently wrong probability is penalised far more than a hedged one, which is the correct incentive for calibrated probability output
layer2.telemetry: Per-game log loss of predicted probabilities against realised outcomes

primitives.name: Multiclass classification is trained with the cross-entropy loss, the negative log of the softmax probability assigned to the true class

symbol_and_unit_ledger.g_y: softmax probability of the true class y, in (0,1)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.z_j: j-th logit, the raw output of the last layer for class j, dimensionless

primitives.verbatim_quote: For the multiclass classification problem, we analogously use the cross-entropy loss function (3.44) as we did for multiclass logistic regression,

assumptions: Input data lives on a grid (image, audio waveform, volume) where nearby entries are more related than distant ones
The same local pattern is worth detecting everywhere in the grid, justifying shared weights
primitives.breakdown_regime: Dense layers on vectorised grid data destroy locality and over-parameterise; convolutions are the wrong inductive bias when position in the grid carries no meaning

layer2.mapping: Structured inputs in the engine (drive sequences, play-by-play grids, formation diagrams) should be processed with structure-aware local operators rather than flattened into unstructured vectors, because locality and translation reuse are real properties of the data
layer2.telemetry: Grid-structured inputs such as play sequences indexed by field position and game clock

primitives.name: Convolutional layers exploit grid structure through sparse interactions and parameter sharing, giving far fewer parameters than a dense layer on the same input
primitives.verbatim_quote: In contrast to a dense layer, a convolutional layer leverages two important concepts – sparse interactions and parameter sharing – to achieve such a parametrisation.

assumptions: Base models have low bias and high variance
Bootstrap resamples approximate drawing new training sets from the population
primitives.breakdown_regime: Variance reduction is floored by the correlation term rho sigma^2: perfectly correlated members gain nothing from averaging, and bagging does not fix a biased base model

layer2.mapping: Engine ensembling follows the variance formula literally: adding another model helps only insofar as its errors are decorrelated from the existing members, so member selection is a correlation decision before it is an accuracy decision
layer2.telemetry: Pairwise error correlations between candidate model families on shared evaluation windows

primitives.name: Bagging averages models trained on bootstrap resamples, reducing the variance of a low-bias high-variance base model without increasing its bias

symbol_and_unit_ledger.B: number of ensemble members, dimensionless count
symbol_and_unit_ledger.rho: average pairwise correlation between ensemble member predictions, dimensionless in [0,1]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.sigma^2: variance of a single member's prediction, squared output units

primitives.verbatim_quote: By using them as base models in bootstrap aggregating, or bagging, we can reduce the variance of the base model without increasing its bias.

assumptions: The training set is a good representation of the population, so resampling it mimics collecting new data
Sampling is uniform over the n training points
primitives.breakdown_regime: Sampling without replacement would just permute the same dataset and produce identical models; the bootstrap understates uncertainty when the original sample is unrepresentative or when data are dependent

layer2.mapping: Resampling historical games with replacement is the engine's uncertainty instrument: refitting on bootstrap seasons gives the sampling distribution of any rating or edge estimate without new data collection
layer2.telemetry: Bootstrap replicate distributions of engine statistics over resampled game sets

primitives.name: The bootstrap creates new datasets of size n by sampling the training data with replacement, so some points repeat and others are omitted
primitives.verbatim_quote: Note that the sampling is done with replacement, meaning that the resulting bootstrapped dataset may contain multiple copies of some of the original training data points, whereas other data points may not be included at all.

assumptions: Base models are decision trees grown by greedy recursive binary splitting
At each split only a random subset of q <= p inputs is eligible
Many trees are averaged or majority-voted
primitives.breakdown_regime: If one dominant variable exists, plain bagged trees all split on it first and stay correlated; too small a feature subset raises individual variance and bias faster than correlation falls

layer2.mapping: Deliberate feature restriction is a decorrelation tool for the engine's model zoo: forcing different model families to build from different signal subsets produces genuinely diverse errors, which is what makes their combination stronger than any member
layer2.telemetry: Feature usage frequencies per ensemble member and member error correlations

primitives.name: Random forests add per-split random feature subsets to bagged trees, lowering the correlation between trees at the cost of higher individual tree variance, with the correlation reduction usually dominating
primitives.verbatim_quote: The idea is to inject additional randomness when constructing each tree, in order to further reduce the correlation among the base models.

assumptions: Each weak learner beats chance on its reweighted training distribution
Binary classification with labels in {-1, 1} in the book's presentation
primitives.breakdown_regime: The underlying exponential loss heavily penalises large negative margins, so AdaBoost deteriorates with label noise and outliers; it is a bias-reduction method and does not fix high-variance base learners

layer2.mapping: Error-focused iteration in the engine mirrors AdaBoost weighting: the games and situations the current model misses most should receive the most analysis weight in the next development round, rather than uniform attention
layer2.telemetry: Per-situation error concentrations from the latest evaluation window

primitives.name: AdaBoost sequentially reweights training points toward those the current ensemble gets wrong, combining weak high-bias learners into a strong one with confidence-weighted votes

symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha^(b): vote weight of the b-th weak learner, dimensionless
symbol_and_unit_ledger.epsilon^(b): weighted training error of the b-th weak learner, dimensionless in (0, 1/2) for a useful learner

primitives.verbatim_quote: Boosting is built on the idea that even a weak high-bias model can often capture some of the relationship between the inputs and the output.

assumptions: A differentiable loss function is chosen for the task
Each stage can approximately fit the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current model
primitives.breakdown_regime: Too many stages overfit; the method inherits sensitivity to the chosen loss, and stage-wise greedy fitting is not jointly optimal

layer2.mapping: The engine's additive adjustments (base projection plus situational corrections) are a boosting-shaped object: each correction should be fit to the residual errors of the running total, not to the raw outcome, and the number of correction layers is itself a fit decision
layer2.telemetry: Residual error of the running projection after each added adjustment layer

primitives.name: Gradient boosting trains an additive model stage by stage, each new basis function fitting the negative gradient of a chosen loss, which generalises AdaBoost to robust losses and regression trees for classification

symbol_and_unit_ledger.B: number of additive terms, dimensionless count
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha^(b): coefficient of the b-th term, dimensionless
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f^(B): the additive model after B stages, output units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f^(b): b-th basis function or weak learner, output units

primitives.verbatim_quote: from a mathematical perspective, a perhaps more useful interpretation is that boosting is as a way to train an additive model.

assumptions: The kernel is positive semidefinite, so a feature map and Hilbert space exist
Predictions are influenced most by training points the kernel deems similar
primitives.breakdown_regime: A default kernel choice silently imposes the wrong function preference; performance still has to be established by cross-validation regardless of theoretical properties

layer2.mapping: Similarity definitions in the engine are priors in disguise: defining two game situations as similar is equivalent to declaring that the projection function should vary smoothly between them, so similarity design deserves the same scrutiny as model design
layer2.telemetry: Similarity matrices over situation feature vectors and their induced neighbourhood outcome rates

primitives.name: A kernel is simultaneously a similarity measure between inputs and a choice of regularisation functional: it encodes which functions are preferred, for example smooth ones for the squared exponential kernel

symbol_and_unit_ledger.kappa: kernel function value, dimensionless similarity in the units of the feature inner product
symbol_and_unit_ledger.phi: feature map into a possibly infinite-dimensional space

primitives.verbatim_quote: The choice of kernel corresponds to a choice of a regularisation functional. That is, the kernel implies a preference for certain functions in the space of all functions that are spanned by the feature vector.

assumptions: Squared error loss with L2 regularisation
The kernel is positive semidefinite so the Gram system is solvable
primitives.breakdown_regime: Every training point is needed at prediction time and the Gram matrix costs O(n^2) storage and O(n^3) factorisation, so the method does not scale to very large n without approximation
primitives.latex: \hat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} = \big(K(X, X) + n\lambda I\big)^{-1} y, \qquad \hat{y}(x_\star) = \hat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^\top K(X, x_\star)

layer2.mapping: A dual, example-based projection layer is viable for the engine at season scale: predictions become weighted sums over historical games with kernel weights, and the weights themselves are inspectable evidence for why a projection leans the way it does
layer2.telemetry: Gram matrices over historical game feature vectors and realised margins

primitives.name: Kernel ridge regression rewrites regularised linear regression in dual parameters, one per training point, with all inner products replaced by kernel evaluations and a closed-form solution

symbol_and_unit_ledger.K(X, X): n by n Gram matrix of kernel values between training inputs
symbol_and_unit_ledger.K(X, x_star): vector of kernel values between training inputs and the test input
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha hat: dual parameter vector of length n, output units per kernel unit

primitives.verbatim_quote: Note that (8.19a) is identical to the corresponding expression for kernel ridge regression (8.14b).

assumptions: The regulariser is a strictly increasing function of the L2 norm of the parameters
The loss depends on the parameters only through predictions at the training points
primitives.breakdown_regime: L1 regularisation breaks the theorem's conclusion, which is why kernel ridge regression could not be derived with an L1 penalty; existence of the dual form does not provide its solution

layer2.mapping: Representation guarantees in the engine should be read with the same discipline: knowing a projection can be expressed through historical examples does not determine the weights; the weighting rule still has to be derived and validated separately
layer2.telemetry: Dual coefficient vectors attached to projections for audit

primitives.name: The representer theorem guarantees that L2-regularised empirical risk minimisers over a feature space have a dual representation in terms of training-point coefficients, but it does not by itself give the dual optimisation problem

symbol_and_unit_ledger.Phi(X): matrix of feature maps of the training inputs
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha hat: dual parameter vector of length n

primitives.verbatim_quote: The representer theorem is a cornerstone of most kernel methods, since it tells us that we can express some models in terms of dual parameters

assumptions: Errors smaller than epsilon are treated as free
L2 regularisation in the primal so the representer theorem applies
primitives.breakdown_regime: Epsilon too large leaves too few support vectors and an underfit model; epsilon too small removes the sparsity and robustness benefit; the dual problem is a constrained optimisation with no closed form

layer2.mapping: An epsilon tube is the right shape for noisy sports outcomes: projection errors inside a tolerance band should cost nothing in model updating, and only games missed by more than the band should drive parameter movement
layer2.telemetry: Counts of games falling outside the tolerance band per model and per situation

primitives.name: Support vector regression uses the epsilon-insensitive loss, which makes the dual parameter vector sparse: only training points outside the epsilon tube, the support vectors, are needed for prediction

symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha: dual parameter vector of length n
symbol_and_unit_ledger.epsilon: half-width of the insensitivity tube, output units

primitives.verbatim_quote: All training data is indeed used at training time (that is, solving (8.19b)), but when making predictions (using (8.19a)), only the support vectors contribute.

assumptions: Binary labels in {-1, 1}
Hinge loss with L2 regularisation in the primal formulation
primitives.breakdown_regime: The predicted margin cannot be interpreted as a class probability, because of the asymptotic minimiser of the hinge loss; multiclass problems need one-versus-rest or one-versus-one constructions

layer2.mapping: Margin-based classifiers in the engine must not have their raw scores read as probabilities: any score that will be presented as a probability needs a separate calibration step, because the training loss determines what the output number means
layer2.telemetry: Score distributions versus realised outcome frequencies for calibration checks

primitives.name: Support vector classification replaces the logistic loss with the hinge loss, whose zero region beyond margin 1 makes the dual solution sparse; it outputs a hard classification, not a probability

symbol_and_unit_ledger.K(X, x_star): kernel values between training inputs and the test input
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha hat: sparse dual parameter vector of length n

primitives.verbatim_quote: Both support vector regression and classification are SVMs since they both have sparse dual parameter vectors.

assumptions: A prior p(theta) is postulated by the user; it cannot be computed from data
A likelihood p(y | theta) is specified
Sequential updating is valid: the old posterior becomes the new prior when more data arrives
primitives.breakdown_regime: Without a meaningful prior the posterior is not meaningful either; for most models the integrals are intractable and need variational or Monte Carlo approximation
primitives.latex: p(y_\star | y) = \int p(y_\star | \boldsymbol{\theta}) \, p(\boldsymbol{\theta} | y) \, d\boldsymbol{\theta}

layer2.mapping: Ratings in the engine are distributions, not points: a team with three observed games carries a wide posterior and its projection should be shrunk and flagged accordingly, with each new game updating the distribution rather than replacing an estimate
layer2.telemetry: Posterior means and spreads per team rating as games accumulate

primitives.name: Bayesian learning replaces a point parameter estimate with the posterior distribution, and prediction marginalises over it, which is why the approach is less prone to overfitting on small datasets

symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(theta | y): posterior distribution over parameters given training outputs
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(y_star | theta): predictive distribution at a test input for fixed parameters
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(y_star | y): posterior predictive distribution, the Bayesian prediction

primitives.verbatim_quote: An interesting and practically relevant consequence is that the Bayesian approach is less prone to overfitting, compared to using a maximum-likelihood based method.

assumptions: Gaussian likelihood with known noise variance sigma^2
Gaussian prior, chosen frankly because it simplifies the calculations
The predictive variance for a new output adds sigma^2 to the function variance
primitives.breakdown_regime: Closed form depends on Gaussian conjugacy; the noise variance and prior variance usually still need choosing, for example by maximising the marginal likelihood

layer2.mapping: The engine's baseline rating model can be exactly this: a Gaussian posterior over team strengths whose width is an honest function of games played, giving projections with defensible uncertainty from the first week of a season
layer2.telemetry: Posterior covariance traces per rating parameter across the season

primitives.name: With a Gaussian prior and Gaussian noise, Bayesian linear regression has a Gaussian posterior and posterior predictive in closed form, with the prior acting as the Bayesian counterpart of regularisation

symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu_0, sigma_0^2: prior mean and prior variance scale
symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu_n, Sigma_n: posterior mean vector and covariance matrix of the parameters
symbol_and_unit_ledger.sigma^2: observation noise variance, squared output units

primitives.verbatim_quote: Just as for plain linear regression, it is possible to use non-linear input transformations, such as polynomials, in Bayesian linear regression.

assumptions: Any finite set of function values is jointly Gaussian
The kernel is positive semidefinite so every finite covariance matrix is valid
The kernel encodes prior beliefs such as smoothness and how correlation decays with distance
primitives.breakdown_regime: Exact inference costs O(n^3); the predictive mean coincides with kernel ridge regression, so the added value is entirely in the variance, which is only as honest as the kernel and noise assumptions
primitives.latex: f \sim \mathcal{GP}(\mu, \kappa), \qquad m_\star = K(X, x_\star)^\top \big(\sigma^2 I + K(X, X)\big)^{-1} y, \qquad s_\star = \kappa(x_\star, x_\star) - K(X, x_\star)^\top \big(\sigma^2 I + K(X, X)\big)^{-1} K(X, x_\star)

layer2.mapping: Projection surfaces in the engine should carry a variance, not just a mean: the Gaussian process construction shows how a similarity kernel over situations induces both, with uncertainty growing away from observed situations, which is the correct geometry for confidence labels
layer2.telemetry: Predictive variances per projection as a function of distance to observed situations

primitives.name: A Gaussian process puts a prior directly over functions, specified by a mean function and a covariance function (kernel); conditioning on observations yields a Gaussian posterior predictive with both a mean and a variance

symbol_and_unit_ledger.kappa: covariance function, equal to the kernel, squared output units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.m_star, s_star: posterior predictive mean and variance at the test input
symbol_and_unit_ledger.sigma^2: observation noise variance, squared output units

primitives.verbatim_quote: However, the Bayesian idea does not only apply to models with parameters but also to nonparametric models.

assumptions: Zero prior mean function in the book's construction
The marginal likelihood is computable in closed form for the Gaussian process
primitives.breakdown_regime: Multiple local maxima mean the optimiser's answer depends on initialisation, and different maxima can be practically different models; maximising the marginal likelihood does not estimate E_new and is not equivalent to cross-validation

layer2.mapping: Hyperparameter selection in the engine has two legitimate routes, marginal likelihood and cross-validation, and they can disagree; disagreement is information about model uncertainty and should be surfaced rather than silently resolved by whichever ran first
layer2.telemetry: Marginal likelihood values and cross-validation errors per hyperparameter candidate

primitives.name: Gaussian process kernel hyperparameters can be selected by maximising the log marginal likelihood, whose surface can have several local maxima corresponding to different interpretations of the data

symbol_and_unit_ledger.K tilde: Gram matrix of the kernel including the noise term sigma^2 I
symbol_and_unit_ledger.eta: vector of kernel hyperparameters such as lengthscale and noise variance
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p_eta(y): marginal likelihood of the training outputs under hyperparameters eta, density units

primitives.verbatim_quote: It is therefore important to carefully choose the initialisation of the optimisation procedure.

assumptions: Class-conditional input distributions are Gaussian
In the supervised case the parameters have closed-form maximum likelihood estimates: class proportions, per-class sample means and covariances
primitives.breakdown_regime: If the Gaussian assumption is badly wrong the derived classifier inherits the error; modelling p(x) is wasteful or infeasible when x is very high-dimensional, such as raw images
primitives.latex: p(x, y) = p(x | y) \, p(y), \qquad p(x | y) = \mathcal{N}\big(x \,|\, \boldsymbol{\mu}_y, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_y\big), \qquad p(y = m) = \pi_m

layer2.mapping: A generative layer over game situations lets the engine ask whether a situation is typical at all, not just what it predicts: atypical inputs get flagged as low-density before any conditional projection is trusted
layer2.telemetry: Densities of incoming game situations under the fitted mixture over historical situations

primitives.name: The Gaussian mixture model is generative: it models the joint distribution p(x, y) as class priors times class-conditional Gaussians, from which the conditional p(y | x) is derived rather than fitted directly

symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu_y, Sigma_y: mean vector and covariance matrix of the input distribution within class y
symbol_and_unit_ledger.pi_m: prior probability of class m, dimensionless, sums to 1 over classes

primitives.verbatim_quote: This is a more ambitious goal than the discriminative classifiers encountered in previous chapters, which only attempt to model the conditional distribution

assumptions: Per-class Gaussian input distributions
For LDA, one covariance matrix shared by all classes, estimated by pooling
primitives.breakdown_regime: QDA estimates a full covariance per class and is data-hungry; LDA and logistic regression often perform similarly but are not equivalent, because their parameters are learned by different criteria

layer2.mapping: Class-conditional modelling of team performance profiles (one distribution per outcome class) is a legitimate lightweight classifier for the engine, with the LDA versus QDA choice reducible to whether classes genuinely differ in spread or only in location
layer2.telemetry: Per-class means and covariances of performance feature vectors

primitives.name: Turning the Gaussian mixture model into a classifier gives quadratic discriminant analysis; forcing a shared covariance across classes cancels the quadratic terms and gives linear discriminant analysis

symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu_m hat, Sigma_m hat: estimated per-class mean and covariance of inputs

primitives.verbatim_quote: Since the logarithm of the Gaussian probability density function is a quadratic function in x, the decision boundary for this classifier is also quadratic, and the method is therefore referred to as quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA).

assumptions: The model contains observed and unobserved (latent) random variables
The expectation and maximisation steps are each tractable
primitives.breakdown_regime: Convergence is to a stationary point, not necessarily the global maximum, so initialisation matters; in the unsupervised mixture case the cluster identities themselves are unobserved and may not correspond to interpretable classes

layer2.mapping: Latent state estimation in the engine (true team strength, hidden game script states) is an EM-shaped problem: alternate between inferring the hidden states given current parameters and refitting parameters given soft state assignments, with monotone likelihood as the sanity check on the implementation
layer2.telemetry: Observed-data log-likelihood trace per EM iteration, required to be non-decreasing

primitives.name: The EM algorithm maximises likelihood in models with latent variables by alternating an expectation step (expected complete-data log-likelihood under current parameters) and a maximisation step; the observed-data log-likelihood increases at every iteration

symbol_and_unit_ledger.y (bold): latent variable vector, here cluster indices

primitives.verbatim_quote: The EM algorithm is a general tool for solving maximum likelihood problems in probabilistic models with latent variables, that is, models containing both observed and unobserved random variables.

assumptions: Data is centred by subtracting the mean
A linear low-rank representation is adequate
By the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem the truncated SVD is the best rank-q approximation in Frobenius norm
primitives.breakdown_regime: Variance is scale-dependent, so variables with dominant units dominate the axes unless standardised; PCA is linear and cannot capture curved structure, which needs the non-linear auto-encoder instead

layer2.mapping: Dimensionality audits of engine feature blocks should start from the singular value spectrum: a feature block whose variance concentrates in two or three directions does not contain twenty independent signals, whatever the feature count says
layer2.telemetry: Singular value spectra per feature block on standardised historical data

primitives.name: Principal component analysis finds the orthogonal directions of largest variance in centred data; the solution is the SVD of the centred data matrix, equivalently the eigendecomposition of the sample covariance

symbol_and_unit_ledger.Sigma: diagonal matrix of singular values in decreasing order, input units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.U, V: orthogonal matrices of left and right singular vectors, dimensionless
symbol_and_unit_ledger.X_0: n by p centred data matrix, input units

primitives.verbatim_quote: Specifically, the first principal axis is the direction with the largest variance; the second principal axis is the direction with the largest variance, but under the constraint that it should be orthogonal to the first principal axis; and so on.

assumptions: Two groups with confusion matrices that the modeller can tune only through the classifier's false and true positive counts
Group base rates are determined by the real world, not by the modeller
primitives.breakdown_regime: The impossibility is structural, not a tuning failure: satisfying two of the three criteria forces the third to differ whenever base rates differ, so fairness claims must name which criterion was chosen

layer2.mapping: Subgroup performance reporting in the engine inherits this constraint: accuracy, hit rate on flagged plays and false alarm rate cannot all be equal across conferences, market types or confidence tiers at once, so reports must state which metric was equalised and which was allowed to differ
layer2.telemetry: Per-subgroup confusion matrices for engine predictions on evaluation windows

primitives.name: It is mathematically impossible for a classifier to simultaneously equalise precision, true positive rate and false positive rate across groups unless base rates are equal or the classifier is perfect on the positive class

symbol_and_unit_ledger.equality condition: the base-rate ratio condition under which all three fairness criteria can hold at once
symbol_and_unit_ledger.n_i: number of negative-class individuals in group i, dimensionless count
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p_i: number of positive-class individuals in group i, dimensionless count

primitives.verbatim_quote: In general, the analysis above shows that it is impossible to achieve simultaneous equality in precision, true positive rate, and false positive rate.

reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: The evaluation layer vetoes everything downstream: no model, however elegant, may be promoted on training performance, because E_train is proven not to estimate E_new. The loss-function layer vetoes interpretation: hinge-trained scores cannot be read as probabilities, and cross-entropy outputs cannot be read as margins. The data layer vetoes splitting choices: group leakage invalidates validation regardless of model quality. And the fairness result vetoes reporting: simultaneous equality of precision, recall and false positive rate across groups is impossible when base rates differ, so any report claiming all three is arithmetically wrong.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage runs from classical statistics into modern machine learning: least squares and Fisher's discriminant from the early twentieth century, the bootstrap and bagging from Efron and Breiman in the 1990s, AdaBoost from Freund and Schapire, support vector machines from Vapnik's statistical learning theory, Gaussian processes from Rasmussen and Williams, and the Bayesian thread from Bayes and Laplace through modern variational and Monte Carlo practice. The authors, all at Linkoping and Uppsala in automatic control, import a systems-engineering sensibility: models are identified from data, validated on held-out data, and only then trusted.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The authors model their reader as an engineer or scientist who knows calculus, linear algebra and basic probability and who will deploy models on real problems with limited time. They believe understanding means being able to derive, not just call, a method: nearly every algorithm is built from a stated model and a loss, and nearly every claim is paired with the regime where it fails. Their model of the domain is that machine learning is an empirical discipline governed by one quantity, expected error on new data, and that most practical failure is evaluation failure rather than algorithm failure.
reasoning_traces.think: This book is a complete first course in supervised machine learning written by four systems-and-control researchers, and its architecture is itself a claim about how the field fits together. It begins with the problem statement: learn a mapping from inputs to outputs from labelled examples, because the true relationship is too complicated to program by hand. It then builds two families of machinery. The first family is discriminative and parametric: linear and logistic regression, generalised linear models, loss functions derived from likelihoods, regularisation in its explicit L1 and L2 forms and its implicit forms such as early stopping and dropout, and the optimisation stack of gradient descent, Newton's method and stochastic gradient descent that makes fitting possible at scale. The second family is structural: decision trees that partition space, ensembles that average or sequentially correct those partitions, kernels that replace explicit feature maps with similarity functions, and finally the Bayesian reformulation in which parameters and even whole functions become random variables with posteriors. Wrapped around both families is the evaluation theory of Chapter 4, which is arguably the book's centre of gravity: the expected new data error E_new is defined as the only quantity that matters, training error is shown to be a biased witness, hold-out and cross-validation are derived as estimators, and the bias-variance decomposition explains why flexibility must be tuned rather than maximised. Chapter 11 then converts the theory into an engineering loop: fix a single-number metric and a validation protocol before iterating, debug by overfitting a tiny subset, diagnose with the training error versus generalisation gap decomposition, and beware group leakage when splitting. For a reasoning engine, the deepest transfer is not any single algorithm but this discipline of evidence. Every engine claim should be traceable to an out-of-sample estimate with a known variance, every similarity definition should be recognised as a regularisation choice, and every probability output should be checked against what its training loss actually licenses it to mean, the hinge loss lesson. The kernel chapters contribute a second deep idea: the representer theorem means a model can be stored as weighted historical examples, which matches how sports reasoning actually talks, in comparable situations, while the Gaussian process chapters show how to attach an honest variance to such example-based predictions, growing with distance from observed situations. The Bayesian chapters contribute the third: parameters as distributions, updated sequentially, with marginalisation as the mechanism that resists overfitting on small samples, exactly the regime of a single sports season. The generative chapters add the ability to model the input distribution itself, enabling typicality checks, semi-supervised use of unlabelled data, and latent-variable fitting by EM. The failure modes are stated as plainly as the methods: E_new is unknowable exactly and shifts with the deployment distribution, grid search collapses combinatorially, marginal likelihood surfaces have multiple maxima with different interpretations, AdaBoost breaks under label noise, and the fairness chapter proves that some desiderata are jointly impossible rather than merely hard. An engine built on this book would therefore be conservative in the right places: aggressive about collecting out-of-sample evidence, explicit about every assumption a number depends on, and silent or hedged where the theory says certainty is unavailable. Chapter 5 deserves separate attention because it is where the book's statistical spine is laid bare: a loss function is not an arbitrary penalty but a modelling choice whose population minimiser determines what the fitted function converges to, so squared error targets the conditional mean, the logistic and cross-entropy losses target class probabilities, the hinge loss targets a margin whose asymptotic minimiser is not a probability, and the exponential loss behind AdaBoost explains its fragility under label noise. This is the book's quiet answer to a question practitioners rarely ask: what does my training objective entitle my output to mean. Chapter 3 makes the same point constructively through generalised linear models, where a link function and a noise distribution turn one linear predictor into regression, classification and count models, with Poisson regression as the worked example. Chapter 10 then shows the generative direction paying rent that discriminative models cannot: because the Gaussian mixture model describes the inputs themselves, unlabelled data becomes usable through the EM algorithm, first semi-supervised and then as clustering, and the same chapter's treatment of normalising flows and adversarial networks shows the transformation view of distributions that modern generative modelling is built on. Chapter 11 adds the practitioner's corrections to naive empiricism: try simple things first, establish baselines and an achievable performance level before iterating, use error analysis on misclassified validation examples to decide what to fix, and when more data cannot be collected, consider augmentation and transfer learning while understanding exactly what each assumes. Chapter 12, written by David Sumpter, closes the loop on the social side of evaluation: performance claims can mislead even without fraud when the test distribution or the metric choice is unrepresentative, training data limitations propagate into deployment harm, and fairness is a property of a chosen error function rather than of the model alone. Computationally, the book is honest about scaling walls: exact Gaussian process inference is cubic, grid search is exponential in the number of hyperparameters, and stochastic gradient descent with backpropagation is presented precisely as the pair of tricks, minibatch gradient estimates and chain-rule reuse, that makes large models fittable at all. What the book deliberately omits is also instructive: reinforcement learning, time series dependence and causal inference sit outside its scope, and its data points are assumed independent throughout, so any engine borrowing its machinery for sequential, dependent sports data must add the dependence handling itself, most urgently in how validation splits respect time and grouping. Taken as a whole, the work functions as a constitution rather than a toolbox: algorithms may be swapped, but the articles, honest out-of-sample evaluation, loss-aware interpretation of outputs, decorrelation as the source of ensemble gains, posteriors instead of points where data is scarce, and impossibility results respected rather than argued with, are meant to bind every later design decision.

universal_lens: Read as a general template, the book says: define the error you will be judged by on data you have not seen, build the simplest model that could work, and let held-out evidence, not fit, arbitrate every increase in complexity. Similarity is a prior, averaging decorrelated attempts reduces variance, sequential correction reduces bias, uncertainty is a distribution rather than a number, and some pairs of goals are jointly impossible for structural reasons. Any prediction system in any domain can be audited with these five questions: what is your E_new estimate, what is your similarity assumption, where does your variance come from, what does your loss license your output to mean, and which of your stated goals are in proven tension.
